savings.note: Savings accounts pay only ~2–8%, fixed deposits ~18–24% (mid-2026) and the CBN’s weighted 3-month deposit rate was ~12% in Jan 2026; 16% assumes a fixed deposit or money-market fund.

balanced.note: Judgement; blend of fixed income (~18–20% T-bills/FDs) and equity.

longTerm.note: NGX ASI rose from ~28,600 (end-2015, from memory — check) to 155,613 (end-2025): ~18% a year in naira, price only.

shares.note: Judgement; NGX returned 37.65% in 2024 and 51.19% in 2025, but long-run returns in naira track inflation plus a few points.

cardApr.note: No published card-rate average found. Bank consumer lending runs ~24–42% (GTBank Quick Credit 2.95%/month ≈ 35.4%); naira cards assumed similar.

loanApr.note: Bank maximum lending rates 32–46% and personal loans 18–36% (mid-2026); 30% is a middle figure.

income.note: Formal-sector survey average ~₦375,000 a month (range ₦150,000–600,000); Lagos formal-sector guides ₦400,000–800,000. Federal minimum wage ₦70,000.

rent.note: Lagos affordable areas ₦50,000–180,000 a month, mid-market ₦120,000–350,000 (Ownkey rental guide; lower-authority source). Rent is paid 1–2 years upfront.

extraFields.label: Generator / inverter fuel
extraFields.help: Petrol or diesel for your generator (or for charging an inverter) when grid power is off, as a monthly amount. Don’t include the cost of buying the generator, inverter or batteries (add those as yearly costs).

single.note: Estimate: small petrol generator ~1 litre/hour, 15–60 litres a month at ~₦1,300 a litre.

suburban.note: Estimate: 60–150 litres of petrol or diesel (₦1,300–1,800 a litre) a month.

extraFields.label: Estate dues and waste bill
extraFields.help: Monthly estate or landlord association dues (security, roads, street lights) and your waste collection bill (for example LAWMA in Lagos). If your service charge is paid yearly, enter it divided by 12.

suburban.note: Estimate; gated estates in Lekki/Ajah can charge far more.

extraFields.label: Ajo / esusu contribution
extraFields.help: Your monthly payment into an ajo, esusu or adashi — a rotating savings group where every member pays in and one member takes the whole pot each round. It works like saving rather than spending, so it is not an essential bill, but count it here so you know where the money goes.

localTips.title: Move from generator to a solar inverter
localTips.why: Generator fuel is often the single biggest power cost in Nigerian homes, and petrol and diesel prices swing with the exchange rate.
tips: Price a 2–5 kVA inverter with lithium batteries and a few solar panels; many vendors offer instalment plans.
Run only fans, lights, TV and router on backup; save heavy loads for grid hours.
Service the generator regularly and switch it off once the inverter is charged.

upfront.note: Small home solar inverter with panels and batteries for lights, fans and a fridge; prices move with the naira.

localTips.title: Get a prepaid meter and check your band
localTips.why: Estimated (“crazy”) billing and paying Band A rates without Band A hours both inflate the electricity bill.
tips: Apply for a prepaid meter through your DisCo’s MAP scheme instead of paying estimated bills.
Track your supply hours for a week; if you get fewer than 20 a day on Band A, complain to the DisCo and NERC.
Buy units through your bank app to avoid vendor charges.

localTips.title: Plan for rent paid a year or two in advance
localTips.why: Landlords usually ask for 1–2 years’ rent upfront, plus agency and legal fees. Enter rent here as the yearly amount divided by 12, and save towards the next payment every month.
tips: Set aside the monthly share of next year’s rent in a separate savings account or money-market fund.
Negotiate the renewal early, before the landlord advertises the flat.
Ask if the landlord accepts rent in two halves instead of one lump sum.
